content.text: Computing Devices, Systems, and Networks

Before understanding how the Internet works, you need to understand the building blocks it is made of: computing devices, computing systems, and computer networks. These three concepts form a hierarchy — devices combine into systems, and networks are a type of system.

content.definition: A physical artifact that can run a program. Examples include computers, tablets, servers, routers, and smart sensors.
A group of computing devices and programs working together for a common purpose. A computer network is a type of computing system.

A group of interconnected computing devices capable of sending or receiving data. A path between two devices is a sequence of directly connected devices that begins at the sender and ends at the receiver.

rows: Computing Device
A physical artifact that can run a program
Computer, tablet, server, router, smart sensor
Computing System
A group of computing devices and programs working together for a common purpose
A school's computer lab network, a company's IT infrastructure, the Internet itself
Computer Network
A group of interconnected computing devices capable of sending or receiving data — a type of computing system
A home Wi-Fi network, a school LAN, the Internet

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: A computer network IS a type of computing system — not the other way around. A computing system is the broader category. Also: routers and servers are computing devices just like computers and tablets — they are physical artifacts that can run programs.
Paths and Routing

When two devices on a network communicate, data must travel from the sender to the receiver along a path. A path is a sequence of directly connected computing devices that begins at the sender and ends at the receiver. There may be many possible paths between two devices — routing is the process of choosing which one to use.

content.definition: The process of finding a path from sender to receiver on a network. Routing on the Internet is usually dynamic — it is not specified in advance.

content.text: Dynamic routing means the path is determined at the time data is sent — not planned in advance. Each router along the way decides the next hop based on current network conditions. This means two packets from the same message might take completely different paths through the network and still arrive at the same destination.

Path is determined in real time as data travels through the network
If the fixed path breaks, data cannot be delivered
If one path breaks, routers find an alternative path automatically

Complex but resilient — adapts to changing network conditions
Not how the Internet works
How Internet routing actually works

content.text: Bandwidth

content.definition: The maximum amount of data that can be sent through a computer network in a fixed amount of time. Usually measured in bits per second.

content.text: Bandwidth is about capacity — it is the maximum amount of data a network connection can carry in a given time period. Higher bandwidth means more data can flow simultaneously. Bandwidth is typically measured in bits per second (bps), kilobits per second (Kbps), megabits per second (Mbps), or gigabits per second (Gbps).

rows: 1 Mbps (1 million bits per second)
Fast enough to browse basic websites and send email
25 Mbps
Minimum recommended for HD video streaming on one device
100 Mbps
Comfortable for a household with multiple simultaneous streams
1 Gbps (1 billion bits per second)
Very high speed — can download large files in seconds

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Bandwidth is the MAXIMUM — not the guaranteed speed. Actual data transfer speeds are often lower than the stated bandwidth due to network congestion, distance, interference, and other factors. Bandwidth is a property of the network connection itself.
The Internet

content.definition: A computer network consisting of interconnected networks that use standardized, open (nonproprietary) communication protocols. Designed to be scalable. Access depends on the ability to connect a computing device to an Internet-connected device.

content.text: The Internet is not a single network — it is a network OF networks. Millions of smaller networks (home networks, school networks, corporate networks, mobile carrier networks) are all interconnected and can communicate with each other because they all use the same standardized, open communication protocols.

content.definition: An agreed-upon set of rules that specify the behavior of a system. The protocols used in the Internet are open, which allows users to easily connect additional computing devices.
Because the protocols used in the Internet are open (nonproprietary), users can easily connect additional computing devices. This is what makes the Internet scalable and accessible to anyone.

content.text: Open (nonproprietary) protocols mean no single company owns or controls the rules of the Internet. Anyone can build a device or service that follows these rules and connect to the Internet. If protocols were proprietary, you would need permission from the protocol owner to connect — which would severely limit the Internet's growth and accessibility.

content.text: Scalability

content.definition: The capacity for a system to change in size and scale to meet new demands. The Internet was designed to be scalable — it can grow to accommodate more devices and users.

content.text: When the Internet was designed, its creators knew it would need to grow. The combination of open protocols and dynamic routing makes this possible. Because protocols are open, anyone can connect a new device without permission. Because routing is dynamic, the network adapts to new devices automatically. The result is a network that has grown from a few research computers in the 1960s to billions of connected devices today — without being redesigned.
How Data Is Sent: Packets

content.definition: A chunk of data with metadata used for routing between origin and destination on the Internet, as well as for data reassembly. Packets may arrive at the destination in order, out of order, or not at all.

content.term: How is data sent through the Internet?
content.definition: Information is passed as a data stream. Data streams contain chunks of data encapsulated in packets. Each packet contains a chunk of data and metadata for routing and reassembly. Packets may arrive in order, out of order, or not at all.
Metadata in a packet is used for two purposes: routing the packet from origin to destination across the Internet, and reassembling the data at the destination once all packets arrive.

content.text: When you send a large file or message over the Internet, it is not sent as one continuous stream. Instead, the data is broken into small chunks called packets. Each packet is then routed independently through the network. At the destination, the metadata in each packet tells the receiving device how to put all the packets back together in the right order — even if they arrived out of order.

rows: Data payload
A chunk of the original message or file
Carries the actual content being transmitted
Source address
Where the packet came from
Tells receivers where to send a reply
Destination address
Where the packet is going
Tells routers how to forward the packet toward its destination
Sequence information
Which piece of the original message this packet represents
Allows the receiver to reassemble packets in the correct order

content.term: What happens if packets arrive out of order or not at all?
content.definition: Packets may arrive at the destination in order, out of order, or not at all. The metadata in each packet is used to reassemble the original data in the correct order regardless of arrival order.

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Because packets may take different paths through the Internet (remember: routing is dynamic), they may arrive at the destination in a completely different order than they were sent. The sequence information in each packet's metadata allows the receiving device to reassemble them correctly. If a packet never arrives, the protocol may request retransmission.
Common Internet Protocols

content.definition: IP (Internet Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) are common protocols used on the Internet. HTTP is a protocol used specifically by the World Wide Web.

rows: IP
Internet Protocol
Handles addressing and routing of packets across the Internet
Every data transmission on the Internet
TCP
Transmission Control Protocol
Ensures all packets arrive and are reassembled correctly — requests retransmission if packets are lost
Web browsing, email, file downloads where accuracy matters
UDP
User Datagram Protocol
Sends packets without guaranteeing delivery or order — faster but less reliable than TCP
Video streaming, video calls, online games where speed matters more than perfect accuracy
HTTP
HyperText Transfer Protocol
Governs how web pages and resources are requested and delivered
The World Wide Web specifically

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: You need to know that IP, TCP, and UDP are common Internet protocols and that HTTP is used by the World Wide Web. You do NOT need to know the detailed technical differences between TCP and UDP for the exam — just that they exist and are Internet protocols.
The Internet vs The World Wide Web

content.definition: A system of linked pages, programs, and files that uses the Internet. HTTP is the protocol used by the World Wide Web. The Web is not the same as the Internet — it is one service that runs on top of the Internet.

content.term: Compare: The Internet vs The World Wide Web
content.definition:
The Internet is the global network of interconnected computers that transmit data.
The World Wide Web is a system of linked pages, programs, and files that runs on top of the Internet using HTTP.
The Web uses the Internet but is not the same thing as the Internet.

content.text: A helpful analogy: the Internet is like the roads and highways of a city. The World Wide Web is like one particular chain of stores you can visit using those roads. There are many other things you can do using the roads (email is like mail delivery, video calls are like phone calls) — the Web is just one of many services that uses the Internet infrastructure.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: The Internet and the World Wide Web are NOT the same thing. The Web USES the Internet, but the Internet is much broader — it includes email, video streaming, online gaming, file transfers, and many other services beyond web pages. HTTP is the protocol for the Web specifically — not the entire Internet.
